text: When you type a prompt to an AI, it doesn't actually see words.
Underneath the interface, it splits your text into small mathematical pieces called tokens.
Each of these tokens is immediately assigned an embedding.
This is a specific row of numbers that represents the token's starting base meaning.
AI works strictly with these numeric tokens.
But to make the exact mechanisms easier to follow today,
we will use whole English words as stand-ins for those numbers.
Because these starting numbers are static, a single token on its own is rigid.
The AI must rely entirely on the surrounding context
to shape that initial math into a final precise meaning.
Context solves two major problems.
First, different meanings.
In please turn on the light, the word means brightness.
Right below, in the empty suitcase felt light, it means not heavy.
Second, ambiguous pronouns.
On the right, it refers to the thirsty cat.
Below, it points to the fresh milk.
The surrounding words are the only mechanism that determines which meaning fits.
Tracking those relationships is the central challenge for any language AI.
Our human brains see the right meaning instantly from the surrounding text.
Earlier AI models, however, had to read text strictly in order.
This graphic illustrates how earlier AI read text.
It followed a linear sequential path,
moving rigidly from left to right, one single word at a time.
By the time this sequential AI reached a pronoun like it,
much later in a long passage, it often struggled to keep the connection
back to the earlier reference word, cat.
Reading linearly breaks down in complex passages,
meaning relies on distant relationships across a sentence,
not just the word that immediately precedes it.
In 2017, eight researchers at Google published a paper called
Attention is All You Need.
This introduced the transformer architecture.
The structure used in modern large language models and the T in chat GBT.
Here, we see how a transformer reads a sentence.
Instead of reading sequentially, the complete message arrives
and is processed in parallel.
Every single word is visible to the system at the exact same time.
Because the whole message is present, a later word like it
can draw information directly from an earlier word like cat,
completely ignoring the several words sitting in between them.
Processing in parallel removes the barrier of distance.
It gives the AI immediate access to the true contextual map of the text.
Taking in the word simultaneously is only the first step.
The AI still has to actively calculate which words matter to one another
to update their underlying numbers.
This chart shows the first mechanism, attention.
The model weighs information from relevant surrounding words
and blends that data directly into the target token's numbers.
Next is transformation.
Here, the AI uses its learned patterns to further process those blended numbers,
reshaping the mathematical identity of the token.
It is important to note that the massive learned weights
inside the AI model stay completely fixed during this step.
What actually changes is the specific role of numbers
representing each individual token in your message.
Attention and transformation work together as an active engine,
building specific meaning from raw context on the fly.
We're turning to our chart on different meanings.
We can see this engine at work.
The surrounding words turn on, provide the exact attention data
the model needs to update the target numbers toward brightness,
while the word empty shifts those numbers toward not heavy.
Looking at the pronouns panel, attention connects the vague word it backward.
It pulls data from the thirsty cat in the first case
and the milk in the second, locking in what the pronoun refers to.
This mathematical synthesis of surrounding context is how the AI successfully locks
in the correct, nuanced meaning of human phrasing.
While attention resolves ambiguous words and pronouns,
processing all this text in parallel creates a new, critical problem,
losing track of word order.
Take the phrases dog bites man and man bites dog.
Without sequence data, these identical tokens just float in the model.
The AI has the words, but cannot tell which came first.
The solution is positional encoding.
The AI stamps every token with a position number, preserving its sequential place.
Positional encoding provides the final necessary piece of architecture.
It tells the transformer exactly where every token belongs in the structure of the narrative.
Modern AI does not read text the way humans do.
It relies on complex mathematical relationships between tokens.
By weighing and blending these numeric relationships,
the AI turns a scattered pile of words into cohesive understanding.
Truly, attention is all you need.
